 Officials warned onlookers to stay off the beaches as waves of more than 50 feet in spots posed hazards. The intense conditions were too dangerous for even seasoned surfers at some beaches.
 Listen · 4:19 min Share full article

 Giant waves at Mavericks in Half Moon Bay, Calif., drew a crowd on Saturday. Waves reaching higher than 50 feet crashed into the Northern California shore. Credit... Mike Kai Chen for The New York Times By Amy Graff and Jesse Klein 
 Amy Graff is a reporter on The Times’s weather team. She is based in San Francisco.
 Published Nov. 14, 2026 Updated Nov. 15, 2026, 4:11 p.m. ET 
 See more of our coverage in your search results. Encuentra más de nuestra cobertura en los resultados de búsqueda. Add The New York Times as a preferred source on Google Agrega The New York Times como fuente preferida en Google › 
 The largest waves in nearly two years pounded the California coast on Saturday, with the intense surf crashing onto beaches and raising the threat of flooding to coastal roads and communities.
 High surf and coastal flood warnings and advisories were in effect along the coast as the National Weather Service advised people to stay out of the water and not even get near it.
 “No selfie of the crashing waves is worth losing your life,” said Roger Gass, a meteorologist at the Weather Service office in Monterey, Calif.
 The tumultuous surf arrived with a powerful swell that was generated by intense winds thousands of miles off the coast and traveled across the Pacific, building energy along the way.
